key_insight: KAISEN shows that subgroup fairness audits can be reproducible yet still fail in specific components, especially when proxy assumptions, calibration choices, or drift thresholds do not transfer across cohorts.
engineering_relevance: For clinical ML deployment, the work highlights that fairness reporting should emphasize subgroup-specific variability, not just average metrics, and that audit thresholds must be validated for each setting.
method: Five-phase audit pipeline: stratify subgroups, measure disparity, diagnose mechanisms, mitigate post-hoc, and monitor drift.
Evaluated on a synthetic benchmark with 16 disease tasks, 15 social-determinant axes, and 3 intersections.
Stress-tested each component to failure with known ground truth.
evidence_signal: On the synthetic benchmark, per-group threshold optimization reduced equalized-odds difference in all 48 held-out runs, while group-wise Platt scaling improved EOD in only 19 of 48 runs and CUSUM false alarms/missed shifts were strongly seed-dependent (chi-squared p = 0.002).
watch_item: Results are entirely synthetic, so the audit conclusions and thresholds may not transfer to real clinical cohorts without revalidation.
paper_title: KAISEN: Reproducible Subgroup Fairness Auditing for Clinical Risk Models
